notes.front: What is generative AI?
notes.back: AI that produces original, human-like content, such as prose, poetry or computer code.
notes.explanation: Microsoft stresses there is no magic in it: it applies mathematical techniques refined over years of research in statistics, data science and machine learning.
notes.example: Like a well-read writer who drafts a new poem on request, rather than a search engine that finds an existing one.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Introduction to generative AI”, “Introduction” (Microsoft Learn training)
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is a large language model (LLM)?
notes.back: A model at the core of generative AI that captures the relationships between words and phrases in a vocabulary and uses them to generate responses.
notes.explanation: It is trained to produce completions from prompts, a far more powerful cousin of the predictive text on a phone.
notes.example: Like an assistant who has read a vast library and can carry on any sentence you begin.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Large language models (LLMs)”, “Large language models (LLMs)” (Microsoft Learn training)
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is a small language model (SLM)?
notes.back: A more compact relation of a large language model that likewise captures relationships between words and phrases.
notes.explanation: Microsoft’s training places large and small language models together at the core of generative AI.
notes.example: Like a pocket dictionary beside a multi-volume one: the same kind of tool, smaller.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Large language models (LLMs)”, “Large language models (LLMs)” (Microsoft Learn training)
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In generative AI, what is a prompt?
notes.back: The input that starts a model’s sequence of text predictions.
notes.explanation: The model carries on from the prompt, predicting the most probable continuation.
notes.example: Like the opening line you give a friend when you ask them to finish a story.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Large language models (LLMs)”, “Predicting completions from prompts” (Microsoft Learn training)
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In generative AI, what is a completion?
notes.back: The output a language model generates by continuing from a prompt.
notes.explanation: Language models are fundamentally trained to generate completions from prompts.
notes.example: Like the reply that finishes a sentence someone else started.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Large language models (LLMs)”, “Predicting completions from prompts” (Microsoft Learn training)
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In a language model’s vocabulary, what is a token?
notes.back: A unit of the vocabulary: a word, part of a word, a punctuation mark or another common sequence of characters.
notes.explanation: People think in words, but models break their vocabulary down into these smaller units.
notes.example: Like building blocks: sentences are made from reusable pieces, some whole words and some fragments.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Large language models (LLMs)”, “Tokenization” (Microsoft Learn training)
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is tokenisation in training a language model?
notes.back: Breaking the training text into its distinct tokens and giving each one a unique integer identifier.
notes.explanation: It is the first step in training a large language model.
notes.example: Like giving each distinct word in a book a catalogue number the first time it appears.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Large language models (LLMs)”, “Tokenization” (Microsoft Learn training)
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In a language model, what is a token’s vector?
notes.back: An array of numbers, such as [4, 9, 2], assigned to the token.
notes.explanation: Each element, or dimension, can encode linguistic and semantic attributes of the token; real models use thousands of dimensions.
notes.example: Like map coordinates, but with far more than two numbers.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Large language models (LLMs)”, “Transforming tokens with a transformer” (Microsoft Learn training)
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is an embedding?
notes.back: A token’s vector after it has been transformed to carry semantic meaning learned from the contexts the token appears in.
notes.explanation: The name comes from the semantic values embedded in the new vectors.
notes.example: Like a word’s reputation, built up from all the company it keeps.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Large language models (LLMs)”, “Transforming tokens with a transformer” (Microsoft Learn training)
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is a transformer model?
notes.back: A model made of an encoder block and a decoder block, used to create embeddings and to predict tokens.
notes.explanation: It turns tokens’ initial vectors into embeddings, then uses those embeddings to generate completions.
notes.example: Like a translator who first studies a text closely, then writes a new one from those notes.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Large language models (LLMs)”, “Transforming tokens with a transformer” (Microsoft Learn training)
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In a transformer, what does the encoder block do?
notes.back: It creates the embeddings, by applying a technique called attention.
notes.explanation: The attention layer’s results go to a fully connected neural network that finds the best vector representation.
notes.example: Like a reader annotating each word with notes about its context.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Large language models (LLMs)”, “Transforming tokens with a transformer” (Microsoft Learn training)
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In a transformer, what does the decoder block do?
notes.back: It uses the embeddings to predict the next most probable token in a sequence started by a prompt.
notes.explanation: The decoder also uses attention and a feed-forward neural network to make its predictions.
notes.example: Like a writer who uses those annotations to choose each next word.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Large language models (LLMs)”, “Transforming tokens with a transformer” (Microsoft Learn training)
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In a transformer, what is attention?
notes.back: A technique that weighs how strongly each surrounding token influences the token being considered.
notes.explanation: The weights are used to calculate the values in that token’s embedding vector.
notes.example: Like reading “the bank of the river” and letting “river”, not “the”, decide what “bank” means.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Large language models (LLMs)”, “Attention and embeddings” (Microsoft Learn training)
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is multi-head attention?
notes.back: Attention that evaluates different elements of the token vectors in parallel.
notes.explanation: Working in parallel makes the encoding process more efficient.
notes.example: Like several proofreaders each checking a different aspect of the same page at once.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Large language models (LLMs)”, “Transforming tokens with a transformer” (Microsoft Learn training)
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is positional encoding?
notes.back: Information fed into the transformer with each token vector, saying where the token appears in the sequence.
notes.explanation: The order in which tokens appear matters to how they relate to one another.
notes.example: Like numbering the pages of a manuscript so it can be read in order.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Large language models (LLMs)”, “Initial vectors and positional encoding” (Microsoft Learn training)
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is a multimodal model, such as a vision-enabled chat model?
notes.back: A model that combines more than one kind of understanding, such as reading images as well as language.
notes.explanation: Vision-enabled chat models, for example, analyse images and answer questions about them in text.
notes.example: Like a colleague you can show a photo to and then ask questions about it.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Use vision-enabled chat models”, “Use vision-enabled chat models” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Vision-enabled chat models are large multimodal models (LMM) developed by OpenAI that can analyze images and provide textual responses to questions about them. They incorporate both natural language processing and visual understanding.

notes.front: What is a reasoning model?
notes.back: A model designed for reasoning and problem-solving tasks, which spends more time processing and understanding the request.
notes.explanation: That extra processing makes such models especially strong in science, coding and maths.
notes.example: Like a chess player who thinks several moves ahead before answering, rather than replying at once.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure OpenAI reasoning models”, “Azure OpenAI reasoning models” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Azure OpenAI reasoning models are designed to tackle reasoning and problem-solving tasks with increased focus and capability. These models spend more time processing and understanding the user's request, making them exceptionally strong in areas like science, coding, and math compared to previous iterations.

notes.front: What is Microsoft Foundry?
notes.back: A platform that unifies agents, models and tools under one management grouping, with built-in enterprise-readiness capabilities.
notes.explanation: Those capabilities include tracing, monitoring, evaluations and customisable enterprise setup.
notes.example: Like a workshop where the tools, the materials and the safety equipment are all kept in one place.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is Microsoft Foundry?”, “What is Microsoft Foundry?” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Microsoft Foundry unifies agents, models, and tools under a single management grouping with built-in enterprise-readiness capabilities including tracing, monitoring, evaluations, and customizable enterprise setup configurations.

notes.front: What is Foundry Models?
notes.back: Microsoft Foundry’s one-stop destination for discovering, evaluating and deploying AI models.
notes.explanation: It serves people building copilots or agents, improving existing applications or exploring new AI capabilities.
notes.example: Like a car showroom where you can browse, test-drive and buy, all in one place.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Microsoft Foundry Models overview”, “Foundry Models” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Microsoft Foundry Models is your one-stop destination for discovering, evaluating, and deploying powerful AI models. Whether you're building a custom copilot, an agent, enhancing an existing application, or exploring new AI capabilities, Foundry Models has you covered.

notes.front: What is the model catalogue in the Foundry portal?
notes.back: The hub for discovering and using a wide range of models to build generative AI applications.
notes.explanation: It lists thousands of models from many providers, including models that Microsoft trained.
notes.example: Like a library catalogue, but for AI models instead of books.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Microsoft Foundry Models overview”, “Overview of model catalog capabilities” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: The model catalog in Foundry portal is the hub for discovering and using a wide range of models to build generative AI applications. The model catalog features thousands of models from providers like Azure OpenAI, Anthropic, Mistral, Meta, Cohere, NVIDIA, and Hugging Face, including models that Microsoft trained.

notes.front: What are Foundry models sold by Azure?
notes.back: Models that Microsoft hosts and sells under Microsoft Product Terms, evaluating them and integrating them deeply into Azure.
notes.explanation: They come from a variety of providers and include direct Microsoft support with enterprise-grade service level agreements.
notes.example: Like a shop’s own-label range: made by various suppliers, but sold and backed by the shop.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Microsoft Foundry Models overview”, “Models sold by Azure” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Microsoft hosts and sells these models under Microsoft Product Terms. Microsoft evaluates these models and deeply integrates them into Azure's AI ecosystem. The models come from a variety of providers and offer enhanced integration, optimized performance, and direct Microsoft support, including enterprise-grade service level agreements (SLAs).

notes.front: What are Foundry models from partners and community?
notes.back: Models provided by trusted third-party organisations, partners, research labs and community contributors.
notes.explanation: They make up the vast majority of Foundry Models.
notes.example: Like the independent sellers on a large shopping site, alongside the site’s own range.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Microsoft Foundry Models overview”, “Models from partners and community” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: These models make up the vast majority of the Foundry Models. Trusted third-party organizations, partners, research labs, and community contributors provide these models.

notes.front: In the model catalogue, what is a model card?
notes.back: A model’s page in the catalogue, with quick facts and tabs of detail such as its benchmarks.
notes.explanation: Benchmark data for a model can be read from its card’s Benchmarks tab.
notes.example: Like the specification sheet pinned to a car in a showroom.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Microsoft Foundry Models overview”, “Overview of model catalog capabilities” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Benchmark data is also available from the model card's Benchmarks tab.

notes.front: In the model catalogue, what is an inference task?
notes.back: The type of task a model performs, such as chat completion, audio generation or embeddings.
notes.explanation: The catalogue lets you filter models by it.
notes.example: Like sorting job applicants by the role they can fill.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Microsoft Foundry Models overview”, “Overview of model catalog capabilities” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Inference task type (for example, chat completion, audio generation, or embeddings)

notes.front: What is the model leaderboard in Microsoft Foundry?
notes.back: A comparison of a curated selection of text-based language models from the model catalogue.
notes.explanation: Models sold by Azure are prioritised, and models must support general-purpose language tasks to be included.
notes.example: Like a league table that ranks teams on several measures at once.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Model leaderboards in Microsoft Foundry”, “Model benchmarking scope” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: The model leaderboards feature a curated selection of text-based language models from the Foundry model catalog. Models are included based on the following criteria: - Foundry Models sold by Azure prioritized : Models sold by Azure are selected for relevance to common generative AI scenarios.

notes.front: On the model leaderboard, what is the quality index?
notes.back: A score where higher means stronger overall performance across reasoning, coding, maths and knowledge tasks.
notes.explanation: Comparing it across models helps identify top performers for general-purpose language tasks.
notes.example: Like an overall grade averaged from several exam papers.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Model leaderboards in Microsoft Foundry”, “Interpret leaderboard results” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: A higher quality index indicates stronger overall performance across reasoning, coding, math, and knowledge tasks. Compare the quality index across models to identify top performers for general-purpose language tasks.

notes.front: In Foundry Models, what is fine-tuning?
notes.back: Tailoring a model that supports it by using data that you provide.
notes.explanation: Only certain models support it, and either managed compute or serverless deployments can be used for it.
notes.example: Like having an off-the-peg suit altered to fit you.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Microsoft Foundry Models overview”, “Fine-tuning models” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Certain models also support fine-tuning. For these models, you can use managed compute or serverless deployments fine-tuning to tailor the models by using data that you provide.

notes.front: In the Foundry model catalogue, what is model retirement?
notes.back: Older models might be retired from the catalogue when a newer version or model in the same family becomes available.
notes.explanation: Some models let you turn on automatic updates to ease the move to a newer version.
notes.example: Like a phone maker ending support for an old handset once its successor is on sale.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Microsoft Foundry Models overview”, “Model lifecycle: deprecation and retirement” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: When a new version or a new model with updated capabilities in the same model family becomes available, older models might be retired in the Foundry model catalog. To allow for a smooth transition to a newer model version, some models let users enable automatic updates.

notes.front: In Foundry Models, what is managed compute?
notes.back: A deployment option where model weights are deployed to dedicated virtual machines.
notes.explanation: One managed compute can hold several deployments, and you’re billed for the virtual machine core hours they use.
notes.example: Like renting your own dedicated server to run the software on.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Microsoft Foundry Models overview”, “Capabilities of model deployment options” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Model weights are deployed to dedicated virtual machines with managed compute. A managed compute, which can have one or more deployments, makes available a REST API for inference. You're billed for the virtual machine core hours the deployments use.

notes.front: In Foundry Models, what is a serverless deployment?
notes.back: A way to consume models through Microsoft-hosted access, without hosting them in your own subscription.
notes.explanation: Microsoft hosts the models in managed infrastructure, which can greatly cut the cost of access and simplify setup.
notes.example: Like streaming a film instead of buying the player and the disc.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Microsoft Foundry Models overview”, “Serverless deployments” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Serverless deployments provide a way to consume Foundry Models as APIs without hosting them on your subscription. Microsoft hosts the models in a managed infrastructure, which enables API-based access to the model provider's model. API-based access can dramatically reduce the cost of accessing a model and simplify the setup experience.

notes.front: In Microsoft Foundry, what does a model’s deployment type determine?
notes.back: Where your data is processed, how you pay, and performance characteristics such as latency variance.
notes.explanation: Deployment types apply to the serverless deployment option.
notes.example: Like choosing a mobile tariff: it decides the network you roam on, how you’re billed and what speeds you get.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Deployment types for Microsoft Foundry Models”, “Deployment types” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: you choose a deployment type that determines: - Where your data is processed (global, data zone, or Azure geography) - How you pay (pay-per-token or reserved capacity) - Performance characteristics (latency variance, throughput limits) These deployment types apply to the Serverless API deployment option.

notes.front: For Data Zone deployment types, what is a data zone?
notes.back: A Microsoft-specified area, such as the United States or the European Union, within which prompts and responses are processed.
notes.explanation: Global types, by contrast, can process prompts and responses in any geography where the model is deployed.
notes.example: Like a postal region: a parcel may travel between towns, but never leaves the region.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Deployment types for Microsoft Foundry Models”, “Data Zone deployments” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: For Global deployment types, the service can process prompts and responses in any geography where the model is deployed. For Data Zone deployment types, the service processes prompts and responses only within the specified data zone:

notes.front: In Foundry deployments, what is provisioned throughput?
notes.back: Reserved processing capacity, bought as a fixed number of provisioned throughput units, that guarantees a set level of capacity.
notes.explanation: It gives lower and more consistent latency than Global Standard.
notes.example: Like booking a dedicated lane on a motorway instead of taking your chances in traffic.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Deployment types for Microsoft Foundry Models”, “Global Provisioned” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: With provisioned throughput, you purchase a fixed number of provisioned throughput units (PTUs) that guarantee a specific level of processing capacity. This deployment type provides lower and more consistent latency than Global Standard.

notes.front: What is the Global Standard deployment type?
notes.back: A pay-per-token type that uses Azure’s global infrastructure to route traffic dynamically to available datacentres.
notes.explanation: It has the highest default quota and removes the need to load-balance across several resources.
notes.example: Like a ride-hailing app that sends whichever driver is free, anywhere in the city.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Deployment types for Microsoft Foundry Models”, “Global Standard” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Global Standard deployments use Azure's global infrastructure to dynamically route traffic to available datacenters. This deployment type provides the highest default quota and eliminates the need to load balance across multiple resources.

notes.front: What is the Global Provisioned deployment type?
notes.back: A type that combines global routing with reserved processing capacity for predictable throughput.
notes.explanation: It guarantees capacity while still routing traffic dynamically to available datacentres.
notes.example: Like a season ticket with a reserved seat, valid at any of the club’s grounds.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Deployment types for Microsoft Foundry Models”, “Global Provisioned” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Global Provisioned deployments use Azure's global infrastructure to dynamically route traffic to available datacenters. This deployment type provides reserved model processing capacity for predictable throughput, combining global routing with guaranteed capacity.

notes.front: What is the Global Batch deployment type?
notes.back: A type for large-scale, high-volume asynchronous work, where many requests are sent together in a single file.
notes.explanation: Jobs are processed asynchronously rather than one request at a time, at a lower cost than Global Standard.
notes.example: Like posting a stack of letters by second-class post instead of sending each by courier.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Deployment types for Microsoft Foundry Models”, “Global Batch” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Global Batch handles large-scale and high-volume processing tasks. You can process asynchronous groups of requests with separate quota and a 24-hour target turnaround, at 50% less cost than Global Standard. With batch processing, rather than sending one request at a time, you send a large number of requests in a single file.

notes.front: What is the Data Zone Standard deployment type?
notes.back: A type that routes traffic dynamically to datacentres within a Microsoft-defined data zone.
notes.explanation: It offers higher default quotas than geography-based types while keeping data within the zone.
notes.example: Like a ride-hailing app that only sends drivers from within your own county.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Deployment types for Microsoft Foundry Models”, “Data Zone Standard” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Data Zone Standard deployments dynamically route traffic to datacenters within the Microsoft-defined data zone (US, EU, or APAC). This deployment type provides higher default quotas than geography-based deployment types while keeping data within the specified zone.

notes.front: What is the Data Zone Provisioned deployment type?
notes.back: A type that routes traffic within a data zone while providing reserved processing capacity.
notes.explanation: It combines data zone compliance with high, predictable throughput.
notes.example: Like a reserved lane on the roads of one region only.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Deployment types for Microsoft Foundry Models”, “Data Zone Provisioned” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Data Zone Provisioned deployments dynamically route traffic within the Microsoft-specified data zone (US, EU, or APAC) while providing reserved model processing capacity. This deployment type combines data zone compliance with high and predictable throughput.

notes.front: What is the Data Zone Batch deployment type?
notes.back: A batch type with the same functionality as Global Batch, but routed only to datacentres within a data zone.
notes.explanation: It keeps Global Batch’s cost saving and turnaround while respecting the zone.
notes.example: Like second-class post that never leaves your region.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Deployment types for Microsoft Foundry Models”, “Data Zone Batch” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Data Zone Batch deployments provide the same functionality as Global Batch, including 50% cost savings and 24-hour turnaround. Traffic is routed only to datacenters within the Microsoft-defined data zone (US, EU, or APAC).

notes.front: What is the Standard deployment type?
notes.back: A type with pay-per-token billing, where you pay only for what you consume.
notes.explanation: It suits low-to-medium volume workloads with high burstiness, though models and throughput per region might be limited.
notes.example: Like a pay-as-you-go phone plan.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Deployment types for Microsoft Foundry Models”, “Standard” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Standard deployments use pay-per-token billing. You pay only for what you consume. Models available in each region and throughput might be limited. Standard deployments are suited for low-to-medium volume workloads with high burstiness.

notes.front: What is the Regional Provisioned deployment type?
notes.back: A type where you specify the throughput you need and the service allocates that processing capacity for you.
notes.explanation: Throughput is measured in provisioned throughput units, a normalised measure.
notes.example: Like reserving a fixed number of desks in one local office.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Deployment types for Microsoft Foundry Models”, “Regional Provisioned” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Regional Provisioned deployments allow you to specify the amount of throughput you require in a deployment. The service then allocates the necessary model processing capacity and ensures it's ready for you. Throughput is defined in terms of provisioned throughput units (PTUs), which is a normalized way of representing the throughput for your deployment.

notes.front: What is the Developer deployment type?
notes.back: A type designed only for evaluating fine-tuned models.
notes.explanation: It gives cost-efficient testing, but no data residency guarantee and no service level agreement.
notes.example: Like a test track: fine for trying a modified car, not for daily commuting.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Deployment types for Microsoft Foundry Models”, “Developer (for fine-tuned models)” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: The Developer deployment type is designed for fine-tuned model evaluation only. It provides cost-efficient testing of custom models but doesn't include data residency guarantees or an SLA. Developer deployments have a fixed 24-hour lifetime and are automatically deleted after expiration.

notes.front: What does the temperature parameter control, and what is its range?
notes.back: How random the model’s output is; it can be set between 0 and 2.
notes.explanation: Higher values give more random, divergent responses; lower values give more focused, concrete ones.
notes.example: Like a dial between “stick to the script” and “improvise freely”.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Prompt engineering with the Chat Completion API”, “Temperature and Top_p parameters” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: The temperature parameter can be set between 0 and 2. A higher value, for example 0.7 makes the output more random and produce more divergent responses, while a lower value, like. 0.2, makes the output more focused and concrete.

notes.front: What is the top_p parameter?
notes.back: A parameter that, like temperature, controls the randomness of a model’s response, but in a different way.
notes.explanation: The general advice is to change only one of top_p and temperature at a time.
notes.example: Like a second dial on the same amplifier: turn one, not both.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Prompt engineering with the Chat Completion API”, “Temperature and Top_p parameters” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Top_probability is another parameter and is similar to Temperature in that it also controls the randomness of the model response, but it does so in a different way. The general recommendation is to alter one of these two parameters at a time, not both.

notes.front: What does the max_tokens parameter do?
notes.back: It limits how many tokens the model’s output can have; output that reaches the limit is incomplete.
notes.explanation: A response stopped this way reports the finish reason `length`.
notes.example: Like a word limit on an essay: the writing stops when it is reached.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Use vision-enabled chat models”, “Output” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: length : Incomplete model output due to the max_tokens input parameter or model's token limit.

notes.front: Roughly how many tokens are in the vocabularies of the latest large language models?
notes.back: Hundreds of thousands.
notes.explanation: They are built from large volumes of training data from the internet and other sources.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Large language models (LLMs)”, “Tokenization” (Microsoft Learn training)
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Besides whole words, tokens include {{c1::sub-words}}, such as the “re” shared by “redo” and “rewrite”.
notes.explanation: Punctuation and other common character sequences can be tokens too.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Large language models (LLMs)”, “Tokenization” (Microsoft Learn training)
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: During tokenisation, what happens when a token that already has an identifier appears again?
notes.back: It keeps its existing identifier; only new tokens get new ones.
notes.explanation: Each distinct token has exactly one identifier, so the vocabulary grows only with new tokens.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Large language models (LLMs)”, “Tokenization” (Microsoft Learn training)
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In an embedding space, how do the vectors of tokens used in similar contexts relate?
notes.back: They point in similar directions.
notes.explanation: The dimensions reflect how tokens relate linguistically, so tokens with similar meanings get vectors that point the same way.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Large language models (LLMs)”, “Attention and embeddings” (Microsoft Learn training)
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which calculation measures how semantically close two tokens are, using their embeddings?
notes.back: Cosine similarity of their vectors.
notes.explanation: It compares the directions in which the vectors point.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Large language models (LLMs)”, “Attention and embeddings” (Microsoft Learn training)
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Similar text produces embedding vectors that are {{c1::close together}}.
notes.explanation: That closeness is what makes embeddings useful for vector search, recommendations, classification and clustering.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure OpenAI embeddings guidance”, “Embeddings” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: An embedding is a vector of floating-point numbers that represents the semantic meaning of text. Similar text produces vectors that are close together, which makes embeddings useful for vector search, recommendations, classification, and clustering.

notes.front: What does an Azure OpenAI embedding consist of?
notes.back: A vector of floating-point numbers that represents the semantic meaning of text.
notes.explanation: You send text to the embeddings endpoint and read the vector back from the response.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure OpenAI embeddings guidance”, “Embeddings” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: An embedding is a vector of floating-point numbers that represents the semantic meaning of text.

notes.front: When attention considers a token, which surrounding tokens get the most weight?
notes.back: The ones that most strongly indicate that token’s meaning in the sequence.
notes.explanation: At first the model doesn’t know which tokens influence others; it learns the patterns from large volumes of text.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Large language models (LLMs)”, “Attention and embeddings” (Microsoft Learn training)
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is masked attention in decoder training?
notes.back: Ignoring the tokens after the current one, so only the preceding tokens form the context.
notes.explanation: Decoder training uses text whose full sequence is already known.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Large language models (LLMs)”, “Predicting completions from prompts” (Microsoft Learn training)
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: During training, how does the decoder improve its predictions?
notes.back: It compares each predicted token with the known next token and adjusts its learned weights to reduce the error.
notes.explanation: Training uses text whose full sequence is already known, so the right answer is available to compare against.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Large language models (LLMs)”, “Predicting completions from prompts” (Microsoft Learn training)
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: After the decoder predicts a token for a completion, what happens next?
notes.back: The token is added to the sequence and the process repeats, until the decoder predicts that the sequence has ended.
notes.explanation: A completion is therefore built one token at a time.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Large language models (LLMs)”, “Predicting completions from prompts” (Microsoft Learn training)
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: At each step of a completion, a language model predicts the next {{c1::most probable}} token.
notes.explanation: The attention layers propose possible vectors and a feed-forward network helps pick the most likely candidate.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Large language models (LLMs)”, “Predicting completions from prompts” (Microsoft Learn training)
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.evidence: For Global deployment types, the service can process prompts and responses in any geography where the model is deployed. For Data Zone deployment types, the service processes prompts and responses only within the specified data zone:

notes.front: A retailer must generate two million product descriptions by next week at the lowest cost, with no need for instant replies. Which type fits?
notes.back: Global Batch.
notes.choices:
A) Global Batch
B) Global Provisioned
C) Standard
D) Developer
notes.choicesExplained: B reserves capacity for steady, low-latency traffic, which this job doesn't need. C is billed per token at the normal price. D is only for evaluating fine-tuned models.
notes.explanation: Global Batch suits large asynchronous jobs, targeting 24 hours at half the cost of Global Standard.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Deployment types for Microsoft Foundry Models”, “Global Batch” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Global Batch handles large-scale and high-volume processing tasks. You can process asynchronous groups of requests with separate quota and a 24-hour target turnaround, at 50% less cost than Global Standard. With batch processing, rather than sending one request at a time, you send a large number of requests in a single file.

notes.front: A trading app sends heavy, steady traffic and needs consistently low latency, with no data residency constraint. Which type fits?
notes.back: Global Provisioned.
notes.choices:
A) Global Standard
B) Global Provisioned
C) Global Batch
D) Data Zone Batch
notes.choicesExplained: A can show more latency variation at high, consistent volume. C and D are asynchronous and target 24 hours.
notes.explanation: Provisioned types reserve capacity and give lower, more consistent latency.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Deployment types for Microsoft Foundry Models”, “Global Provisioned” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: With provisioned throughput, you purchase a fixed number of provisioned throughput units (PTUs) that guarantee a specific level of processing capacity. This deployment type provides lower and more consistent latency than Global Standard.

notes.front: You’ve fine-tuned a model and want a cheap way to try it out today. Which deployment type is designed for this?
notes.back: Developer.
notes.choices:
A) Developer
B) Regional Provisioned
C) Data Zone Standard
D) Global Batch
notes.choicesExplained: B reserves throughput capacity and isn't designed for evaluating fine-tuned models. C is for pay-per-token use within a data zone. D is for large asynchronous jobs.
notes.explanation: The Developer type exists only for evaluating fine-tuned models, and lasts 24 hours.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Deployment types for Microsoft Foundry Models”, “Developer (for fine-tuned models)” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: The Developer deployment type is designed for fine-tuned model evaluation only. It provides cost-efficient testing of custom models but doesn't include data residency guarantees or an SLA. Developer deployments have a fixed 24-hour lifetime and are automatically deleted after expiration.

notes.front: An app writes exact safety instructions for factory machines. Should its temperature be set high or low?
notes.back: Low, for more focused and concrete output.
notes.explanation: Lower values make output more focused and concrete, and less random.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Prompt engineering with the Chat Completion API”, “Temperature and Top_p parameters” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: The temperature parameter can be set between 0 and 2. A higher value, for example 0.7 makes the output more random and produce more divergent responses, while a lower value, like. 0.2, makes the output more focused and concrete.

notes.front: You’ve raised temperature to get more varied answers, and now also want to change top_p. What does the guidance recommend?
notes.back: Leave top_p alone: alter one of the two at a time.
notes.explanation: The guidance is to alter one of these two randomness controls at a time, not both.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Prompt engineering with the Chat Completion API”, “Temperature and Top_p parameters” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Top_probability is another parameter and is similar to Temperature in that it also controls the randomness of the model response, but it does so in a different way. The general recommendation is to alter one of these two parameters at a time, not both.

notes.front: Answers keep stopping mid-sentence, with the finish reason `length`. Which parameter should you raise?
notes.back: `max_tokens` (or `max_completion_tokens` for o-series reasoning models).
notes.explanation: That finish reason means the output hit the token limit.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Use vision-enabled chat models”, “Output” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: length : Incomplete model output due to the max_tokens input parameter or model's token limit.

notes.front: How does a transformer’s encoder block differ from its decoder block?
notes.back: The encoder builds embeddings using attention; the decoder uses those embeddings to predict the next most probable token.
notes.explanation: Both use attention, but for different jobs: one to understand context, the other to generate.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Large language models (LLMs)”, “Transforming tokens with a transformer” (Microsoft Learn training)

notes.front: How does a small language model differ from a large language model?
notes.back: It is a more compact relation of the large model; both capture the relationships between words and phrases.
notes.explanation: The difference the training material draws is one of size, not of kind.

notes.front: Who supports models sold by Azure, compared with models from partners and community?
notes.back: Microsoft supports models sold by Azure; partner and community models are supported by their providers, with varying service levels.
notes.explanation: Support expectations are one of the factors to weigh when choosing between the two categories.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Microsoft Foundry Models overview”, “Choosing between models sold by Azure and models from partners and community” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Models sold by Azure come with robust Microsoft-provided support and maintenance. Partner and community models are supported by their providers, with varying levels of SLA and support structures.

notes.front: How does billing differ between managed compute and serverless deployment?
notes.back: Managed compute: the virtual machine core hours used. Serverless: inputs and outputs, typically in tokens.
notes.explanation: With managed compute you run the machines; with serverless, Microsoft hosts the model for you.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Microsoft Foundry Models overview”, “Capabilities of model deployment options” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: You're billed for the virtual machine core hours the deployments use. Access models through a deployment that provisions an API. The API provides access to the model that Microsoft hosts and manages for inference. You're billed for inputs and outputs to the APIs, typically in tokens.

notes.front: How does data processing differ between Global and Data Zone deployment types?
notes.back: Global: in any geography where the model is deployed. Data Zone: only within the specified data zone.
notes.explanation: Data Zone types keep processing inside the chosen zone, such as the European Union.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Deployment types for Microsoft Foundry Models”, “Data Zone deployments” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)

notes.front: How do Standard and provisioned deployment types differ in billing and latency?
notes.back: Standard: pay-per-token, with latency that may vary. Provisioned: reserved capacity, with low latency variance.
notes.explanation: The choice follows from whether a workload can accept variation in latency.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Deployment types for Microsoft Foundry Models”, “By latency requirement” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-ai-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Low latency variance required : Use Provisioned types - Latency variance acceptable : Use Standard types
